name: Yáo’ān Central Yi
confidence_why: The quoted passage has not been checked against the cited source.
catalog_citation: Merrifield, W. Scott. 2012. Yáo’ān Central Yi Phonology. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2012-002 (May 2012; Glottolog lists it as 2012-003). Dallas: SIL International. 21 pp.
catalog_locator: Section 4 'Syllable Stress', p. 10 (whole section, exx. 56-60); tones Section 2.1, p. 6; Section 8 'Intonation and Breath Groups', p. 17.
catalog_quote: Stress is not contrastive for Yáo’ān Central Yi. The tone (pitch level) of the syllable and syllable stress are related in that, when there is a two-syllable utterance, the syllable with the higher tone carries slightly greater stress. If the tones are the same, syllable stress is the same for both syllables. In this context the term "stress" implies loudness. It has also been noted that no significant lengthening of the vowel has been observed occurring with increased syllable stress. In addition, greater stress on a syllable can raise the tone. For example, there is a set of time-related phrases in Yáo’ān Central Yi that are glossed as: ‘then; later; next; at that time’, and in all such cases the final syllable is stressed. This final syllable carries a slightly higher pitch than normal. ... 56. næ55 po55 næ55 ‘but at that time’ is pronounced næ55 po55 næ66
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lolopo (Yao'an Central Yi, Mayou) is a three-tone language (21, 33, 55) in which stress is non-contrastive and has no fixed position: perceived loudness simply tracks tone height (the higher-toned syllable of a disyllable sounds slightly stronger; equal tones give equal prominence), with no vowel lengthening; the only positional effect noted is final-syllable prominence with slight pitch raising in a small set of time-adverbial phrases.
new_statements.exceptions: A set of time-related connective phrases ('then; later; next; at that time', e.g. næ55 po55 næ55) carry stress on the final syllable, realized with slightly raised pitch (55 -> '66'). Tense vowels also raise pitch slightly (33->44, 55->66), independent of stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns 'syllable stress' within two-syllable utterances/words and short phrases; sentence-level intonation and breath groups treated separately in Section 8. Variety: Loxrlavu of Mayou village west of Yao'an, Chuxiong Prefecture, Yunnan.
new_statements.identity_note: Merrifield 2012 describes the Loxrlavu/Loxrlovu (lo̠ʔ21 la33 vʊ33) variety of Mayou village west of Yao'an city, Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan -- i.e. Yao'an Lolopo proper, squarely lolo1259 [ycl]. Hayashi 2015, which Glottolog also files under ycl, instead describes the 'Lolopho' of Muang Sing, Luang Namtha, Laos (migrants from Nyot-U, Phongsali); its identity with Yunnan Central Yi is asserted by the author only tentatively and should not be used for lolo1259 without care. Easterday 2019's appendix entry that cites Merrifield 2012 is coded for Sichuan Yi (Nuosu, nuos1239), not Lolopo.

sources.note: Section 4 'Syllable Stress' (p. 10): stress is not contrastive; three phonemic tones (21/33/55); in a two-syllable utterance the higher-toned syllable is slightly louder, equal tones = equal stress; no vowel lengthening under stress; in a set of time-adverbial phrases the final syllable is stressed and its pitch slightly raised (55 -> '66').
